input: Nobody in our scenario reported trying another tool. My switching hypothesis, not a finding, is that a link in the existing chat could save the organizer from chasing answers without asking members to install anything. Synthetic scenario: the 2 committed members agreed to try an availability-link prototype with us before judging. We do not know why the other 3 had no problem. This is a free club activity with no buyer or payment plan. If a simple shared link does not help those two coordinate without chasing, that would weaken our idea; if everyone prefers the existing chat, we should investigate rather than build a new app. Here is facilitator-supplied desk research, not research by the coach and not student field evidence: source https://workspace.google.com/intl/en/products/forms/ , accessed 2026-09-09. Paraphrased page findings: Google says Forms collects survey responses, shows response charts, and exports raw data to Google Sheets. This does not establish that it solves our club scheduling problem. We could investigate using a form link or continuing the current manual chat process. We have six hours, one beginner coder, and one business student.
output:
Established: Switching hypothesis (labeled as hypothesis, not a finding): a link in the existing chat could let members self-report availability without the organizer chasing answers or installing anything new. No club member has tried an alternative tool before. This is a free club activity with no buyer/payment plan. The 2 committed members will try an availability-link prototype before judging. Desk research (attributed to Google, the vendor): source https://workspace.google.com/intl/en/products/forms/, accessed 2026-09-09 — Forms collects survey responses, shows response charts, and exports to Sheets; this does not establish fit for your scheduling problem. Team resources: six hours, one beginner coder, one business student.

Still unknown: the exact action the 2 participants will take, the observable measurement, and the precommitted success/failure threshold for the prototype test.

1. What specific action will the 2 committed members take with the availability-link prototype (e.g., click a link and mark open times, reply to a form)?
2. What will you actually observe or measure (e.g., whether they settle on a time without further chasing, how many back-and-forth messages it takes, whether the session happens)?
3. What threshold, set before the test, would count as a disappointing result using that same measurement (e.g., "if they still need more than one follow-up message to settle a time, that's disappointing")?
